Identifying Key Challenges in Ovarian Tumor Classification:
A Comparative Study Using Deep Learning and Radiomics
Eloy W.R. Schultza, Terese A.E. Hellstr¨oma, Cris H.B. Claessensa, Anna H. Kochb, Joost
Nederendc, Ilse Niers-Stobbed, Annemarie Bruininge, Jurgen M.J. Piekb, Peter H.N. De Witha,
and Fons van der Sommena
aDepartment of Electrical Engineering, Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven, The Netherlands
bDepartment of Obstetrics and Gynecology and Catharina Cancer Institute,
Catharina Hospital, Eindhoven, The Netherlands
cDepartment of Radiology and Catharina Cancer Institute, Catharina Hospital, Eindhoven, The Netherlands
dDepartment of Radiology, Amphia Hospital, Breda, The Netherlands
eDepartment of Radiology, Antoni van Leeuwenhoek Hospital, Amsterdam, The Netherlands
ABSTRACT
Ovarian tumor malignancy classification is a challenging task for radiologists using current algorithms, as they
do not reach the required accuracy for clinical decision-making. The heterogeneous nature of ovarian tumors
makes differentiation more difficult compared to other classification tasks, such as e.g. lung-nodule classification,
even for experienced radiologists. The integration of computed tomography (CT) data with deep learning holds
potential to improve accuracy, but its application remains in its infancy, where most previous work relies on
radiomic feature extraction. This study compares a radiomics-based model and two deep learning models across
both ovarian and lung datasets.
The results demonstrate that although these models are promising, there
is considerable variation in performance across the classification tasks, which reflects their level of difficulty.
The performed feature analysis shows that ovarian tumors exhibit high feature heterogeneity and lack feature
robustness, underscoring the need for novel methods to enhance feature differentiation. However, it is also shown
that it is possible to gain performance for a majority of cases, by identifying features that can filter out outliers.
Furthermore, the obtained results suggest that tumor volume plays a clear role in ovarian tumor classification,
where large malignant tumors are most difficult to classify. These findings highlight that there is no one-size-fits-
all solution to deep learning for tumor classification in CT, as model performance depends heavily on the task.
Tailoring models to address dataset-specific challenges is critical to advancing their clinical utility. The code for
our work is published on GitHub at: https://github.com/EloySchultz/OvaCADx_SPIE2025.
Keywords: Ovarian tumor classification, Multiple instance learning, Radiomics, Computed tomography, 3D
CNN, Dataset comparison
1
INTRODUCTION
Ovarian cancer ranks as the sixth most lethal cancer among women in the United States, with an estimated
12,740 deaths in 2024 and a five-year relative survival rate of approximately 50%, making it the most fatal
gynecologic cancer.1 Its high mortality rate is primarily driven by the late-stage diagnosis in more than 50%
of all cases, largely due to the vague and non-specific symptoms associated with the disease in its early stages.
Accurate pre-operative differentiation between benign and malignant ovarian tumors is crucial because their
treatment and prognoses differ substantially. Patients with early-stage ovarian cancer require specialized care in
oncology centers, while those with benign tumors can be managed in non-oncologic hospitals.
Currently, clinical models based on ultrasound are used to pre-operatively differentiate between benign and
malignant tumors. However, these models lack discriminative power and rely heavily on the skill and experience
of the operator.2,3
Furthermore, they typically prioritize sensitivity at the cost of high false positive rates,
leading to unnecessary oncology referrals, negatively impacting patient outcomes and increasing patient stress.4
Volumetric imaging models offer an alternative that reduce reliance on operator expertise, since volumetric
imaging relies on standardized, computerized techniques that produce consistent results. Computed tomogra-
phy (CT) stands out compared to Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), due to its shorter imaging times and its

greater widespread availability and accessibility.5 Moreover, CT imaging is primarily recommended for assessing
metastatic disease,6 emphasizing its established role in the pre-operative evaluation of ovarian tumors, making
it important to explore its potential for classification as well. However, the extraction of correct diagnoses from
CT images remains challenging. Ovarian tumors exhibit substantial variability in size, shape and enhancement
pattern, while benign and malignant tumors often appear visually similar on CT, as highlighted in Figure 1.
The high variance and similarity complicate the distinction of benign and malignant tumors from CT images.
Computer-aided diagnosis (CADx) can play a crucial role in overcoming these challenges by leveraging ad-
vanced techniques, such as radiomics7 and deep learning. Radiomics enables the extraction of high-dimensional
quantitative features from medical images, while deep learning models can learn complex patterns and represen-
tations directly from the data, thereby offering the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and consistency.
Previous studies in ovarian tumor classification are predominantly based on handcrafted radiomic features for
classification, which have reported area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) values between 0.66 and 0.97
for CT-based approaches8–13 and 0.82 to 1.0 for MRI-based methods.14–19 However, many of these results are
undermined by the absence of independent training, validation, and test datasets, or the use of insufficient cross-
validation techniques.20 Moreover, most studies rely on single-center datasets without external validation, raising
concerns about overfitting and limiting generalization. Despite the growing interest in deep learning methods,
their application to ovarian imaging remains limited, particularly with CT datasets. To date, only a few studies
explore deep learning models, reporting a wide range of AUCs (0.84-0.99).13,21–23 This underscores the need for
more robust methodologies and broader exploration of deep learning approaches for ovarian tumor classification.
In this study, two deep learning models for classifying malignant and benign ovarian tumors are evaluated
and their performances are compared against a radiomics-based approach. To minimize validation bias, nested
cross-validation and an independent test set from an external center are used for evaluating the models. Due
to the lack of publicly available ovarian tumor datasets, the models are also benchmarked using a public lung-
nodule dataset. This approach enables a comparison with existing literature and offers insights into differences
in classification difficulty between the two datasets. Additionally, this performed study analyzes which features
most significantly influence model performance, by identifying subsets of ovarian tumors for which classification
performance is improved. These evaluations aim to enhance understanding of the factors inducing classification
performance, and contribute to improved diagnostic strategies for ovarian cancer management.
The contributions of this work are threefold and listed below.
1. Gaining deeper insights into the performance differences and challenges associated with ovarian tumor
classification, by analyzing an ovarian tumor dataset and a lung-nodule dataset.
2. Two deep learning classification methods for ovarian tumors, which are employed and compared with a
radiomics-based method.
3. Identification of relevant features that heavily influence classification performance, which are found by
selective subset filtering.

METHODS
2.1
Datasets
In this study, each model is trained on two primary CT-scan datasets to assess their efficacy on different clas-
sification tasks. The first dataset is an ovarian tumor dataset, which serves our primary application in this
work: computer-aided diagnosis (CADx) of ovarian masses. The second dataset concerns a different CT-based
CADx application, i.e. lung-nodule characterization, for which numerous reliable benchmark results are already
available. This renders it an excellent application to serve as a reference for model performance in a comparable
CADx task.
Ovarian tumors: Our ovarian cancer dataset consists of retrospectively collected pseudonymized CT scans
from three medical centers: Amphia Hospital Breda (BRE), Catharina Hospital Eindhoven (CZE) and The
Netherlands Cancer Institute - Antoni van Leeuwenhoek Hospital Amsterdam (AVL), all located in The Nether-
lands. Data from the first two centers are used for training, validation and internal testing, whereas data from
the third center are used as an external test set. The dataset consists of CT scans containing 400 lesions from
356 patients in total, with the distribution across the centers and classes given in Table 1. Patients with two tu-
mors of different nature are excluded, as well as patients with borderline tumors. Manual lesion annotations are
made by medical research fellows, supervised by medical experts, where ground-truth diagnoses are determined
from histopathology results. The CT scans are obtained by CT scanners of 4 brands (GE Medical Systems,
Philips, Siemens, Toshiba). The majority of scans (≥80%) is portovenous, but some are nephrogenic, delayed
and non-contrast enhanced. The CT scans have a 12-bit dynamic range of [-1024,+3071] Hounsfield units (HU)
and have a size of (512×512×Z) voxels, where the number of slices Z represents the scan length capturing the full
lesion. All scans are resampled to 3-mm slice thickness if necessary. The average spacing is (0.739×0.739) mm2
with an interquartile range of 0.119 mm.
Lung nodules: The second dataset is the public Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Re-
source Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) dataset, obtained from The Cancer Imaging Archive, consisting of 1018 CT scans
of patients with lung nodules gathered from seven academic centers located throughout the United States.24 We
adopt a radiologist-consensus strategy25 to obtain ground-truth malignancy of the nodules using the PyLIDC
library.26 Scans are discarded when clustering fails, or when there are less than 4 assigned annotations. The
resulting dataset contains 638 lesions (Table 1).
2.2
Preprocessing of the data
For training, validation and testing, we employ 5×5 nested cross-validation to evaluate model performance, as
shown in Figure 2. The outer loop stratifies the data into 5 testing/training folds, while the inner loop further
stratifies each extracted training set in 5 validation/training folds. This means that in total, each model is
trained 25 times. This approach is particularly effective because it leverages all data points multiple times across
different roles, ensuring that model performance metrics are less influenced by specific data splits. The validation
folds are used to determine the early stopping point during training. Bilateral tumors of the same nature are
treated as a single entity during data splitting. The voxel intensities for the ovarian and lung-nodule datasets
are windowed over the ranges [-200, +300] and [-1000, +400] HU respectively,27 based on the HU values in
the relevant tissues. All tumors are randomly flipped along all three axes during training to facilitate model
generalization across different views.

2.3
Evaluation
Model performance is assessed using three metrics: the AUC under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC)
curve, sensitivity, and specificity. To calculate the AUC, the floating-point predictions of the inner loop models
are averaged, resulting in one prediction for each sample in the test set. The predictions from each outer loop
test set are then pooled. A bootstrapping approach is applied, where samples are drawn with replacement,
comprising one-fifth of the pooled test set. The AUC is calculated on these selected samples. This bootstrapping
process is repeated 1,000 times, yielding an empirical distribution for the AUC.
Similarly, a bootstrapping approach is used to calculate the sensitivity and specificity. While any operating
point on the ROC curve may be selected, we estimate optimal cut-off thresholds by maximizing the F1 score on
the validation data.28 After applying these thresholds, majority voting among the inner loop binary predictions
is used to obtain a single binary prediction for each sample in the test set. The empirical distributions for
sensitivity and specificity are then derived using the same bootstrapping process as for the AUC. An exception
is the subset analysis, where the AUC is calculated on the average of the inner loop predictions directly without
bootstrapping, resulting in a single AUC value for each subexperiment.
The results are presented with three decimal places to reflect the precision gained from bootstrapping 1,000
times for each experiment, though we acknowledge that limitations in dataset size may affect the reliability of
the third decimal.
2.4
Feature comparison
The datasets are analyzed using radiomic feature analysis29 involving extraction of 1,316 radiomic features
from the annotated regions, following the method by Li. et al.9 The discriminative power of each feature is
assessed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) distance metric.30
Our analysis evaluates both the interclass
differences between benign and malignant ovarian tumors and the intraclass differences between the training and
validation fold within the malignant class. Features with low between-class KS similarity are highly effective
in distinguishing benign and malignant ovarian tumors and features with high within-class KS similarity show
consistency and robustness across different configurations of the validation folds.
2.5
Models
We have selected three classification models based on their suitability for ovarian tumor classification: (1) 3D con-
volutional neural network (3DCNN) for its ability to leverage the spatial context of 3D data, (2) MIL for its
ability to focus on relevant slices, and (3) a radiomics-based approach due to its prevalence in the literature.
Details for each of these models are provided in the following sections.

2.
Multiple instance learning convolutional neural network (MILCNN). This approach uses slice-

in Figure 3. This allows the model to focus on slices containing the most relevant information, while removing

3.
Radiomics with a neural network.
In this approach, a neural network is used to make predictions
using radiomic features (Radiomics + NN). The feature selection pipeline is based on the approach of Li. et al.9
with some adaptations.
Following univariate analysis, image features are iteratively selected, based on the
least Pearson-Spearman correlation with features that are already selected, rather than applying a correlation
threshold. Pearson correlation is calculated when both variables exhibit normality according to the Shapiro-Wilk
test (p > 0.05); otherwise, Spearman correlation is calculated. Additionally, automated knee-point selection is
employed to determine the optimal number of features during feature elimination. This involves identifying the
point on the “number of features vs. accuracy”-curve that is furthest from a line fitted to the entire curve.35
Based on the selected features, a two-layer fully connected neural network is trained for classification.
2.6
Subset analysis
As ovarian tumors are inherently heterogeneous, we examine the impact of intrinsic radiomic features on classifier
performance. We hypothesize that the models may be biased towards certain features, and that excluding outliers
can enhance the performance for the majority of patients. To investigate these potential biases, we analyze each
feature independently, testing various subset compositions on our validation dataset. In this process, for each
radiomic feature, the data are first sorted by feature value and then split into two subsets based on the feature
median. One subset contains data points with feature values above or equal to the median, while the other
contains data points with feature values below the median. The AUC is computed for both groups using the
malignancy probabilities predicted by the MILCNN+R model on the validation dataset. The maximum AUC
from the two groups (AUCmedian) is recorded, and the group with the higher AUC is selected.
To investigate how the AUC develops if the size of the subset changes, we manually select 5 features of
interest [f1, f2, f3, f4, f5] that are distributed over the full AUCmedian range. We introduce a fraction T that
controls the subset size relative to the full dataset. The percentile threshold is then adjusted such that the
selected subset is T times the size of the full dataset. Note that the selected subset is either above or below
the threshold, based on the performance observed at the 50-th percentile cut. For each value of T, the AUC
is calculated using the malignancy probabilities predicted by the MILCNN+R model on this selected subset of
the validation dataset. This allows us to assess how the AUC varies with different feature thresholds. We then
select a value for T and evaluate it on the test set.

3
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1
Feature comparison
The KS similarity distributions depicted in Figure 4 reveal that the ovarian dataset exhibits high between-
class KS similarity, indicating many features poorly differentiate between benign and malignant ovarian tumors.
Furthermore, the within-class similarity is generally lower, suggesting great heterogeneity within each class
and less feature robustness.
In contrast, the LIDC-IDRI dataset shows uniformly distributed between-class
similarity, with low-similarity features effectively distinguishing between classes. Additionally, the high average
within-class similarity in LIDC-IDRI reflects more class-robust features. These results suggest that ovarian tumor
classification may be inherently more challenging due to less distinct feature separability, highlighting the need
for advanced techniques to enhance feature differentiation compared to lung-nodule datasets.
3.2
Classification results
For all evaluated models, their performances on the LIDC-IDRI dataset consistently surpass the values obtained
on the ovarian dataset, as shown in Table 2. The AUCs that are obtained on the LIDC-IDRI dataset (0.921 −
0.960) are comparable to those found in literature (0.951−0.987).36–38 Compared to the ovarian dataset results,
the test set interquartile range of the LIDC-IDRI dataset results is smaller, indicating higher model stability for
the LIDC-IDRI models. These disparities may be attributed to the feature heterogeneity of the ovarian dataset
described previously, complicating accurate automated classification.
This highlights the need for continued
research in ovarian tumor classification, given its increased complexity compared to lung-nodule classification.
For the ovarian dataset, the MILCNN outperforms the 3DCNN, likely due to the MIL’s ability to handle
noise and artifacts by discarding irrelevant slices and focusing only on slices that are indicative of malignancy.
Notably, the 3D rotational augmentations have a positive effect on classification performance for both deep
learning models, and for both the internal and the external AUC of each model. Comparing radiomics to deep
learning shows that both the Radiomics+NN method and the MILCNN+R method seem effective at classifying
ovarian tumors, hence both methods should be considered for further development.
The results in Table 2
also show a discrepancy between internal and external test set scores, emphasizing the necessity for evaluating
models on both types of datasets to ensure reliability prior to clinical implementation. The applied radiomics-
based model achieves an AUC of 0.810, which is notably lower than the range of values reported by other
CT-based radiomics approaches in the literature (0.83-0.97),8–13 including the 0.91 achieved by Li et al.,9 despite
our efforts to replicate their method as closely as possible. Similarly, our best deep learning performance, with
an AUC of 0.815, is on the lower side of AUC values reported in literature for CT (0.84-0.99).13,21–23 However,
direct comparisons remain challenging due to the lack of publicly available datasets, which limits consistent
benchmarking. This highlights the urgent need for standardized datasets to enable meaningful performance
comparisons and accelerate progress in the field.

3.3
Subset analysis
The distribution of AUCmedian across all radiomic features, calculated with the logits of the MILCNN+R model
is shown in Figure 5A. The majority of features have an AUCmedian higher than the baseline of 0.815 (Table 2),
suggesting that the model has developed bias towards most features. These results show that many features
capture a promising characteristic for identifying a subset of patients where the model obtains a superior AUC
value. The highest performing feature f1, which is the voxel-based tumor volume, achieves an AUC of 0.90 on
the low-volume validation set, and 0.888 on the low-volume test set. In total, 85 features exist with a valida-
tion AUCmedian higher than 0.90, showing high potential for outlier detection and removal. In clinical practice,
outliers excluded by feature-based outlier filtering would require additional evaluation by clinical experts, since
the limited data available for these cases makes it difficult for the model to generate reliable predictions.
The five manually selected features are further analyzed for different subset sizes, as shown in Figure 5B.

Examining the features with the highest AUCmedian qualitatively∗, we observe that many features are related
to tumor volume (volumetric features, energy-based features). This is an interesting finding, since ovarian tumors
vary considerably in size and are in general substantially larger than lung nodules. To further elaborate on the
effect of size on ovarian tumor classification performance, we select feature f1 (voxel-based tumor volume) as
the principal feature and the median volume as the corresponding threshold T=0.5. We then evaluate both
small-tumor and large-tumor subsets, with the results presented in Table 3. The table shows that a size bias is
evident for the ovarian dataset, because the AUC for the small-tumor subset is considerably higher than for the
large-tumor subset. Additionally, the class accuracy indicates that large malignant ovarian tumors are notably
harder to classify. On the LIDC-IDRI dataset, the subset performance is lower than that of the full dataset,
with the small subset predominantly consisting of benign samples and the large subset of malignant samples,
thereby highlighting the correlation between size and malignancy in lung nodules. These findings suggest that
tumor size is a key factor for automated malignancy prediction of the ovarian tumor class, with smaller tumors
yielding higher performance. In contrast, for lung nodules, size alone is often highly indicative for malignancy.
4
CONCLUSION
Ovarian tumor classification using CT-scan images presents significant challenges compared to certain other
tumor classification tasks, such as lung-nodule classification, primarily due to the heterogeneity and low feature
robustness of this tumor type. We have developed multiple classification methods and have evaluated them both
on an ovarian dataset and a well-established LIDC-IDRI dataset as a benchmark. The analysis of the obtained
results highlights the substantial variability in radiomic feature distributions, underscoring the heterogeneous
nature of ovarian tumors on CT scans, which complicates classification. Despite this challenge, the findings of the
experiments demonstrate that both radiomics-based and deep learning-based methods show potential for effective
ovarian tumor classification. This finding holds particularly when techniques such as rotation augmentations are
employed to improve model generalization. Additionally, the performed study identifies a high number of features
that strongly impact classification performance, highlighting the potential for feature-based subset selection as
a strategy to improve performance for the majority of patients.
Many high-performing features are related
to tumor volume. When dividing the ovarian tumors into a low-volume and a high-volume group, it can be
observed that large ovarian tumors, especially large malignant tumors, are more difficult to classify accurately,
indicating tumor size as a key factor influencing performance. In contrast, in lung-nodule data the nodule size
alone forms a strong prediction for malignancy. The experiments emphasize the importance of understanding
dataset variability and the related difficulty in developing effective classification models. For challenging tasks
like ovarian tumor classification, refining the problem statement by developing models for a subset of the patient
distribution can enhance performance and clinical applicability.

Abstract: Ovarian tumor malignancy classification is a challenging task for radiologists using current algorithms, as they do not reach the required accuracy for clinical decision-making. The heterogeneous nature of ovarian tumors makes differentiation more difficult compared to other classification tasks, such as e.g. lung-nodule classification, even for experienced radiologists. The integration of computed tomography (CT) data with deep learning holds potential to improve accuracy, but its application remains in its infancy, where most previous work relies on radiomic feature extraction. This study compares a radiomics-based model and two deep learning models across both ovarian and lung datasets. The results demonstrate that although these models are promising, there is considerable variation in performance across the classification tasks, which reflects their level of difficulty. The performed feature analysis shows that ovarian tumors exhibit high feature heterogeneity and lack feature robustness, underscoring the need for novel methods to enhance feature differentiation. However, it is also shown that it is possible to gain performance for a majority of cases, by identifying features that can filter out outliers. Furthermore, the obtained results suggest that tumor volume plays a clear role in ovarian tumor classification, where large malignant tumors are most difficult to classify. These findings highlight that there is no one-size-fits- all solution to deep learning for tumor classification in CT, as model performance depends heavily on the task. Tailoring models to address dataset-specific challenges is critical to advancing their clinical utility.
